youtube_title: Too Rich for a Roth IRA? The 'Backdoor' Explained 🦝⚖️
caption: Direct Roth IRA contributions have income limits; conversions don't. The 'backdoor' pairs a nondeductible traditional IRA contribution with a conversion — but existing pre-tax IRA money can make part of it taxable.
script: The IRS says you're too rich for a Roth IRA. Then it hands you the instructions to get one anyway. [disclaimer] People call it the backdoor! This is American tax law. A Roth IRA is a retirement account people love, because if you follow the rules, the money you take out later isn't taxed. Nice! But putting money straight into a Roth has income limits. Make too much money, and you can't put money in directly. Sorry! But converting is different. The IRS says, no matter how much you make, you may be able to move money from a regular IRA into a Roth. So the backdoor is just two steps. Step one, put money into a regular IRA, and don't take a tax deduction for it. Step two, convert that money into a Roth. Done! You report it on an IRS form, Form eighty six oh six. Here's what the quick videos skip. The normal yearly limits still apply. You need income from work to put money in at all. A conversion taxes any money that hasn't been taxed yet. And if you already have pre tax money sitting in regular IRAs, the IRS counts all of it together, so part of your conversion can still get taxed. And once you convert, there's no undo button. This is an explanation, not advice. Talk to a tax pro before moving retirement money. [loop] So if someone tells you high earners can't have a Roth, remember
